description:
We are MLIoT_HKT, a passionate team of young innovators participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our team is interested in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), software development, and space technology.

Our project focuses on developing an intelligent health monitoring system for astronauts by combining wearable health data, space environmental data, and data analysis to support health assessment and risk awareness during space missions.

We believe technology can help address real-world challenges in space exploration. Through creativity, teamwork, and interdisciplinary collaboration, we aim to transform complex data into meaningful insights and practical solutions.

We welcome passionate individuals with skills in AI/ML, IoT, data science, software development, UI/UX design, and space science who are eager to innovate, learn, and contribute to the future of space exploration.

Together, let's turn ideas into impactful solutions beyond Earth!
summary:
Our project develops an intelligent astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to address the challenges of maintaining human health during space missions.

The system integrates physiological data from wearable devices, space radiation information from NASA and NOAA, and self-reported health assessments into a unified platform. By analyzing health trends over time and combining them with environmental risk indicators, the application helps astronauts identify potential health concerns and better understand their physical and psychological well-being.

Beyond traditional health monitoring, our solution provides personalized health insights, interactive visualizations, and step-by-step guidance for manual health measurements. It also supports self-assessment procedures when communication with Earth is unavailable.

Our project addresses a critical challenge in space exploration: transforming complex health and environmental data into actionable insights that support astronaut autonomy.
details:
## AstroVitals: Health Monitoring for Astronauts

AstroVitals is a prototype health-monitoring app for astronauts and the doctors supporting them from Earth. Crew members can log health check-ins and symptoms, review trends and measurement guidance, and see relevant space-weather information. A Ground view lets a flight surgeon review incoming reports and send a response. Health readings in the prototype are simulated and are **not for medical decisions**.

### How it works

The app is a progressive web app (PWA) designed to keep working when a crew member is offline. Check-ins and reports are stored on the device; reports wait in an outbox and sync when the connection returns. The app also includes a communications simulator to demonstrate delays or loss of contact. It can display live space-weather data from NOAA and NASA, while clearly distinguishing that data from simulated health readings.

### Benefits and intended impact

AstroVitals explores how a single tool could help crews keep track of their wellbeing and help ground teams respond to reports despite communication delays. It brings check-ins, trends, measurement instructions, space-weather context, and crew-to-ground reporting together. The intended impact is to support more informed monitoring and coordination on long-duration missions, where timely contact with Earth may not always be possible.

### Tools, languages, and hardware

The frontend uses React and TypeScript, built with Vite as an offline-capable PWA. It stores local data in the browser with IndexedDB and Dexie, and uses Three.js for 3D visual elements. The backend is written in Go and uses PostgreSQL; Docker Compose runs the services together. Space-weather information comes from NOAA SWPC and NASA DONKI. An optional Anthropic API integration is available for a limited AI-assisted feature.

The project does not build or connect custom physical hardware. Instead, it models workflows around spaceflight measurement equipment—such as thermometers, pulse oximeters, activity monitors, dosimeters, and cabin sensors—and includes simulated readings for demonstrations.

### What makes it creative, and what the team considered

AstroVitals combines health tracking with offline-first design, space-weather context, and a ground medical workflow in one app. It uses a 3D body map, measurement guides, and optional quests to make the interface more engaging and understandable. The team considered unreliable communications, the need to prioritize urgent reports, the clarity and traceability of measurement guidance, and the difference between real environmental data and simulated health data.
